item.description: Le pape Léon XIV a promis dimanche de reprendre progressivement ses fonctions à la tête de l'Eglise catholique lors de sa première apparition publique depuis son opération subie il y a cinq jours pour un cancer du poumon.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Le pape Léon XIV a promis dimanche de reprendre progressivement ses fonctions à la tête de l'Eglise catholique lors de sa première apparition publique depuis son opération subie il y a cinq jours pour un cancer du poumon. "Après avoir surmonté cette phase délicate (...), je vais maintenant reprendre peu à peu mes activités, toujours avec l'aide de Dieu et grâce à vos prières", a déclaré le souverain pontife, s'adressant d'une voix ferme et claire, depuis une fenêtre du palais apostolique du Vatican, à des milliers de fidèles rassemblés place Saint-Pierre. Agé de 71 ans, Léon XIV a subi mardi une opération visant à lui retirer le lobe inférieur du poumon droit après détection d'une tumeur maligne. Ce diagnostic, pour un pape connu pour être relativement jeune et énergique et qui n'a été élu qu'en mai 2025, a soulevé des questions quant à l'avenir de son pontificat alors qu'il doit faire face à la maladie.

item.title: EU condemns attacks by violent settlers, including on diplomats, spokesperson says
item.description: The European Union "strongly condemns" attacks by violent settlers in the West Bank, including against European diplomats, the bloc's foreign policy spokesperson said on Sunday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The European Union "strongly condemns" attacks by violent settlers in the West Bank, including against European diplomats, the bloc's foreign policy spokesperson said on Sunday. The statement came a day after Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot said Israeli settlers attacked Palestinian civilians, European diplomats and a French mayor in the occupied West Bank. "We take positive note of statements by several Israeli representatives who condemned the attacks but we expect full accountability as well as effective measures to prevent continued acts of violence and violent harassment against Palestinians, including during the ongoing olive harvest season, as well as against journalists," the EU spokesperson said.

item.title: One killed, 15 injured in Ukrainian drone attack on St Petersburg and Leningrad region
item.description: Ukrainian drones struck oil facilities and logistics and data centers, local authorities said.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: One person was killed and 15 were injured in a Ukrainian drone attack on oil facilities, logistics and data centres in Russia's St Petersburg and the Leningrad region, local authorities said on Sunday. St Petersburg's governor Alexander Beglov said fires had broken out at the St Petersburg oil terminal, an oil depot and industrial warehouses. Russian e-commerce company Ozon said that its logistics hub in St Petersburg was on fire and the internet company VK (VKCO.MM) said that its data centre in the Leningrad region had been attacked by drones, but services were available to users as normal. Ukrainian drone producer Fire Point said on Sunday that the Ukrainian military had struck a VK data centre near St Petersburg. Russian air defence units downed 1,015 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions overnight, the Russian Defence Ministry said. Russia is constantly responding to Ukrainian attacks with systematic, large-scale strikes, the TASS news agency reported on Sunday, citing Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov. "The Kyiv regime is resisting. But this cannot change the course of events," he said, answering a question about how Russia might respond to Kyiv's attack on St Petersburg.

item.title: IMF/World Bank meetings leave developing countries with more questions than answers
item.description: Last week's meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank yielded no new answers for the developing world to the questions posed by a spreading Middle East war, continuing war in Ukraine, rising debt payments and a potential AI bubble.
item.dc:creator: Andrea Shalal, David Lawder
item.content:encoded: Last week's meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank yielded no new answers for the developing world to the questions posed by a spreading Middle East war, continuing war in Ukraine, rising debt payments and a potential AI bubble. Not for the first time, [USN:L1N46302K TEXT:"lower-income countries"] are being rocked by the spillover from the actions of wealthier nations: rising debt service costs, higher inflation and the risk of falling ever further behind economically thanks to the AI boom. What they got was the stock advice the global lenders always dish out: to shrink fiscal deficits and accelerate economic reforms to attract more private sector investment. Kristalina Georgieva, the first IMF chief from a developing nation - Bulgaria - said advanced economies were in fact the worst offenders on budget imbalances. She noted that developing countries' debt levels had actually fallen in recent years, only for surging bond yields elsewhere to drive up their borrowing costs. Average debt service payments there had more than doubled from a decade ago to 14% of government revenue, crowding out education, healthcare and other critical areas, she said. ADVANCED ECONOMIES FOCUSED ON THEIR OWN PROBLEMS At a panel on Saturday, Georgieva said many issues remained unresolved, especially around AI: "We are in a place where we have many more questions than we have answers. And my alert to everybody is: Do not fall for the guys that pretend they have the answers. They are tricking you." Josh Lipsky, vice president of international economics at the Atlantic Council think tank, said the meetings had flunked their opportunity to come up with guidance or ways to help. "It's hard to talk about the developing world when the advanced economies don't have their act together and are at risk of a fiscal crisis," he said. "And that's on top of political situations in many of these countries that makes development aid not a priority at the moment." Mauricio Cardenas, Colombia's former finance minister and now a research scholar at Columbia University's School of International and Public Affairs in New York, said many policymakers were left with a deep sense that "something really bad could happen" but no real roadmap to navigate the future. "The IMF and World Bank are not particularly well prepared for this new phase. They understand that something is going on, they bring in experts on AI," he said. "But in the end, there's no kind of specific, concrete advice on how to be prepared for something where you don't really understand how it's going to unfold." The geopolitical tensions that have roiled both institutions since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 - complicating concerted action - were also evident in Bangkok when nearly half the delegates at an [USN:L1N46301V TEXT:"IMF steering committee"] walked out when Russia's finance minister spoke. Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport delayed the arrival of the head of that committee, Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed Al-Jadaan, who had to travel overland to Qatar to catch a flight. And Bangkok itself was a stark reminder of the challenges facing developing countries, still partly under water after floods in September that caused almost $200 million in damage to Thailand's industrial sector. RISING INEQUALITY COULD RAISE COSTS IN LONG TERM Kate Pickett, a professor at the University of York, urged policymakers to focus on more inclusive growth rather than forcing developing countries into tough structural reforms. "If inequality increases, if poverty deepens, that will increase their costs in the long term," she said. "It's not enough to describe an economy as resilient. It's only resilient for the rich and the privileged.” Ayhan Kose, deputy chief economist at the World Bank, said the global economy had weathered its biggest energy shock - from the US-Israeli war on Iran - better than expected. But while a global recession had been avoided, he said growth outlooks in both developing and advanced economies were worse than before. Growth had already fallen off in half of advanced economies, while in developing countries as a whole, it had slowed significantly to around 3.6% from 4.4%. “People are really worried because resilience today is not a guarantee for resilience tomorrow," he said. "Now they are worried about what will be the next shock, because every six months, if not every three months, there is a new shock." While no specific initiatives were announced, he said the World Bank remained focused on helping developing countries prepare for advancements in AI, in part by mobilising more private capital, now at triple the levels of 2022. Yet it, too, has to contend with sharp drops in official development aid and persistent challenges in attracting foreign investment to developing countries. “The reality on the ground is the reality on the ground,” he said.

item.title: L'Egypte prête à contribuer à la sécurité de l'Arabie saoudite
item.description: L'Egypte est prête à apporter à l'Arabie saoudite le soutien nécessaire à la défense de sa sécurité et de sa stabilité face aux attaques des Houthis, a déclaré dimanche la présidence égyptienne.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: L'Egypte est prête à apporter à l'Arabie saoudite le soutien nécessaire à la défense de sa sécurité et de sa stabilité face aux attaques des Houthis, a déclaré dimanche la présidence égyptienne. Le président égyptien Abdel Fattah al Sissi a demandé la tenue d'une session parlementaire dans la journée afin d'autoriser l'armée égyptienne, l'une des plus importantes et des plus puissantes de la région, à contribuer à la défense du royaume si celui-ci en faisait la demande. "L'Egypte apportera à l'Arabie saoudite toutes les formes de soutien nécessaires et possibles pour défendre sa sécurité et sa stabilité, protéger ses ressources, son intégrité territoriale et les lieux saints de l'islam", a déclaré la présidence égyptienne dans un communiqué. Ces derniers jours, les Houthis, soutenus par l'Iran, ont pris pour cible l'aéroport international de Ryad ou encore des installations de la compagnie publique pétrolière Aramco. L'Egypte et l'Arabie saoudite sont des partenaires stratégiques et économiques étroits. Ryad et d'autres pétromonarchies du Golfe ont fourni à l'Egypte des aides se montant à des milliards de dollars après le renversement par l'armée du président islamiste Mohamed Morsi en 2013.

item.title: Iran urges US to accept proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz
item.description: Iran's offer to the United States to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days is still on the table, Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told Iranian media outlets on Sunday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Iran's offer to the United States to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days is still on the table, Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told Iranian media outlets on Sunday. Iran presented its proposal in mid-September after an [USN:L1N42P0Q6 TEXT:"interim ceasefire"] collapsed. Tehran later acknowledged receiving a US response but [USN:L1N45X04L TEXT:"Iran’s security chief"] said last week negotiations have stalled because Washington failed to address all [USN:L1N45Q01J TEXT:"seven conditions"] for reopening the strait. "Our situation is clear and based on the seven-days proposal presented to the US. They shared comments which we are reviewing, but our proposal is still on the table and if there is any honesty on the US part, which there isn't, the way to reopening the Strait of Hormuz is obvious," Araqchi said while in Baghdad for a meeting of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. Iran's conditions include, among other demands, the lifting of the US blockade on its ports, the lifting of US sanctions on its oil exports as well as ending hostilities on all regional fronts. If Washington accepts Tehran's conditions, the strait could reopen within six days, with talks resuming the following day, Araqchi said. A central point of disagreement has been Washington’s insistence on addressing Iran's [USN:L1N45T0JD TEXT:"nuclear programme"] from the outset. US Vice President JD Vance said earlier this month that Iran must make a "meaningful" reduction in its uranium enrichment capacity to satisfy US demands and end the countries' eight-month war. Tehran says negotiations should initially focus on reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which before the war carried about a fifth of the global trade in oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG), and restoring security in the waterway.

item.title: Accenture looks to sell Chinese operations for up to $1.5 billion, FT reports
item.description: IT consulting firm Accenture is looking to sell its Chinese operations for up to $1.5 billion, the Financial Times reported on Sunday, citing people familiar with the matter.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: IT consulting firm Accenture (ACN.N) is looking to sell its Chinese operations for up to $1.5 billion, the Financial Times reported on Sunday, citing people familiar with the matter. Reuters could not immediately verify the report. Accenture has hired JPMorgan (JPM.N) to work on a strategic review of the China business after receiving unsolicited interest in the unit over the past year, the report added. Accenture and JPMorgan did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment outside regular business hours. The sale process is likely to draw interest from private equity groups and a small cluster of strategic buyers, the report said. Accenture may opt to retain a significant minority stake in the business, the report added. Accenture’s Greater China operations include Taiwan, Hong Kong and mainland China, according to its website. The consultancy firm recently forecast full-year 2027 revenue growth between 3% and 6%, above analysts' estimates.

item.title: Egypt says ready to give Saudi Arabia necessary support amid Houthi conflict
item.description: Egypt is ready to provide Saudi Arabia with the support it needs to defend its security and stability, the presidency said on Sunday, as Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis intensify their attacks on the world's largest oil exporter.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Egypt is ready to provide Saudi Arabia with the support it needs to defend its security and stability, the presidency said on Sunday, as Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis intensify their attacks on the world's largest oil exporter. Egyptian President [USN:L8N46306J TEXT:"Abdel Fattah al-Sisi"] requested an urgent parliament session to authorise the military, one of the Arab world's largest, to help defend Saudi Arabia if the kingdom requested its support. A parliamentary vote had been expected on authorizing the request for military support on Sunday, but discussions were due to continue on Monday, two lawmakers and local media reports said. HOUTHIS RAMP UP ATTACKS ON SAUDI ARABIA The Houthis have in recent days attacked [USN:S8N44Y00K TEXT:"Riyadh's international airport"] and the state oil giant [USN:S8N44D022 TEXT:"Saudi Aramco"], amid renewed fighting with the Saudi-backed forces of the internationally recognised government following the collapse of a truce. "Egypt will provide Saudi Arabia with all necessary and possible forms of support to defend its security and stability, protect its resources, territorial integrity and Islamic holy sites," the Egyptian presidency said in a statement. It followed a meeting of Egypt's National Defence Council chaired by Sisi and attended by the parliamentary speaker, the prime minister and the army chief. Sisi said in a [USN:L8N46306J TEXT:"speech"] on Saturday that Egypt would act in accordance with guidance from Saudi King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who visited Sisi on September 15, after fighting in Yemen reignited. Egypt and Saudi Arabia are close strategic and economic partners. Saudi Arabia and other oil-rich Gulf states provided Egypt with billions of dollars in aid, central-bank deposits and investments after the military ouster of Islamist President Mohamed Morsi in 2013. Egypt had previously joined the Saudi-led coalition that intervened in Yemen in 2015 to support the government against the Houthis, but played a limited combat role.

item.title: Pope Leo pledges gradual return to duties in first event since cancer surgery
item.description: Pope Leo pledged on Sunday to slowly resume his usual activities as the leader of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics as he greeted crowds in St. Peter's Square during his first public event since undergoing surgery for lung cancer five days ago.
item.dc:creator: Joshua McElwee
item.content:encoded: Pope Leo pledged on Sunday to slowly resume his usual activities as the leader of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics as he greeted crowds in St. Peter's Square during his first public event since undergoing surgery for lung cancer five days ago. The 71-year-old pontiff had an [USN:S8N42Y05U TEXT:"operation"] on Tuesday to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, [USN:L8N4600P9 TEXT:"fuelling speculation"] about how his illness might change his 17-month papacy. Smiling from a window of the Vatican's Apostolic Palace as he spoke to pilgrims below in a firm, clear voice on Sunday, the first US pope thanked people across the world for their prayers and said he would now begin to resume his normal schedule. "Having overcome this delicate phase... I will now gradually resume my activities, always with the help of God and your prayers," Leo said. The pope, who was discharged from Rome's Gemelli hospital on Saturday, came to the window in the palace unaided and held his weekly midday appointment as usual. He also urged pilgrims waiting below under cloudy skies to set aside any selfish ambitions and serve God "without compromise". NUN CRIES AS LEO MAKES APPEARANCE Leo has been diagnosed with [USN:L8N46006S TEXT:"lung adenocarcinoma"], the most common form of lung cancer. The diagnosis, for the youngest pope in decades, who was elected only in May 2025, caused shock. His doctors discharged him on Saturday after blood tests and chest imaging that day showed him well enough to return home. They said he was able to perform normal daily activities independently. Crowds in St. Peter's Square, numbering about 15,000 according to the Vatican, shouted and clapped loudly as Leo first appeared at the window on Sunday. One Catholic nun knelt and cried, holding her hand over her face. A few steps away, a group of other nuns held aloft a sign reading, "Best wishes, Holy Father. We love you and we are praying for you". POPE'S CALENDAR IN FLUX Leo usually keeps a busy schedule, but the Vatican has cancelled his other public events until at least Wednesday, when he is due to hold a weekly general audience in St. Peter's Square. It has not said whether he will hold that audience. The pope is also planning to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17, in one of the most intense trips arranged for a Catholic leader [USN:L8N45D0VL TEXT:"in decades"]. Dr. Stefano Margaritora, the pope's lead surgeon, said on Saturday that Leo could be fully recovered in time for that trip. Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican's secretary of state, has however expressed scepticism. He told journalists on Friday the pope may need to adjust the pace of his schedule going forward "according to the condition of his health".

item.title: Paris condamne l'agression d'un maire français par des colons juifs
item.description: La France a condamné dimanche l'agression "gravissime" par des colons juifs du maire d'Aulnoye-Aymeries survenue la veille dans le village palestinien de Taybeh.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: La France a condamné dimanche [USN:L8N46309E TEXT:"l'agression"] "gravissime" par des colons juifs du maire d'Aulnoye-Aymeries survenue la veille dans le village palestinien de Taybeh. Dans un communiqué, le Quai d'Orsay a exprimé "son soutien et sa solidarité" à l'égard des représentants de plusieurs missions diplomatiques, dont le consul général de France à Jérusalem et ses homologues belge et polonais également pris à partie lors de cette attaque. "La France appelle les autorités israéliennes à arrêter les auteurs de cette agression gravissime et à les traduire en justice. Au-delà, les autorités israéliennes doivent prendre toutes les mesures nécessaires pour faire cesser ces actes de terreur", a souligné le ministère des Affaires étrangères. "La France réitère sa condamnation de la politique de colonisation. La colonisation est contraire au droit international. Elle porte une atteinte grave aux droits des Palestiniens, menace la stabilité de la Cisjordanie et compromet la solution à deux Etats", a-t-il ajouté.

item.title: Roy Cooper's North Carolina playbook is working. Can other Democrats copy it?
item.description: North Carolina hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate in nearly 20 years, but former Governor Roy Cooper, who hasn't lost an election in four decades, has built a double-digit lead over Republican Michael Whatley.
item.dc:creator: Yasmeen Abutaleb
item.content:encoded: North Carolina hasn’t elected a Democrat to the US Senate in nearly 20 years, but former Governor Roy Cooper has built a double-digit lead over Republican Michael Whatley by relentlessly focusing on affordability and a blunt promise to “make stuff cost less.” At campaign stops, Cooper, 69, points to his six-year fight to expand Medicaid through a Republican-controlled legislature as evidence he can work across party lines, while attacking Trump-backed healthcare cuts that he says are hitting North Carolinians hard. “People should not have to make a choice between going to a doctor and putting food on the table,” Cooper said at a September 26 rally in Raleigh, North Carolina. “This 'Big Beautiful Bill' that gave tax cuts to billionaires has now driven healthcare premiums up more than double for people.” The White House says the bill cuts taxes, protects Medicaid for eligible Americans and curbs fraud and abuse. Cooper's message appears to be working: His lead stood at 14 points in an October SurveyUSA poll. The top super PAC for Senate Republicans has paused TV advertising in North Carolina less than three weeks before the election and begun shifting campaign dollars to defend seats in states that include Iowa and Kansas. President Donald Trump will rally in the state on Tuesday for Whatley, a former Republican National Committee chair who has never held elected office. The question for Democrats is whether Cooper's playbook can help them win Republican and independent voters elsewhere, or whether his success is unique to a popular former governor who has never lost an election in four decades of public service. While some Democrats in heavily Democratic states have embraced Medicare for All, which would provide government-run health insurance for all Americans, Cooper has focused on expanding existing coverage and lowering costs. He points to his fight to expand Medicaid, the government health insurance program for low-income Americans, and campaigns on prescription drug and insurance costs. 'OUR STAR ATHLETE AND NO ONE'S PAYING ANY ATTENTION' “It’s like he’s our star athlete and no one’s paying any attention,” said Neera Tanden, president of the Center for American Progress, a Democratic-aligned think tank, and former White House adviser to President Joe Biden. “The strength of Roy Cooper’s campaign is that he’s able to attract Democrats and independents, but also even some Republicans because he’s focused on cost, but he also has a record.” Paul Shumaker, a longtime Republican strategist in North Carolina, attributes Cooper’s success to the fact he was already well-known and that Whatley failed to distinguish himself from Trump. “Roy Cooper came to the US Senate race with a known brand that has been trusted by a majority of North Carolina voters election after election,” Shumaker said. “Republicans are suffering from a lack of trust on the economy right now and Whatley has failed to reestablish that trust.” Cooper declined an interview request for this story. The Whatley campaign did not respond to a request for comment, but on Sunday he predicted victory during an interview with Fox News. Trump's upcoming visit to North Carolina and an expected rally with Vice President JD Vance will energize Republican voters, Whatley told Fox News' "Sunday Briefing." "Our election is going to come down to turnout and we're in a state that President Trump won three straight times," Whatley said. WINNING OVER INDEPENDENTS North Carolina’s electorate is unusually independent: 40% of registered voters are unaffiliated with either party, compared with 30% each for Republicans and Democrats. Republicans, however, have dominated the state legislature for more than a decade and redrawn districts to strengthen their grip. Like other Republican candidates, Whatley must contend with Trump’s record-low approval rating, which now hovers at 32%, according to an October [USN:L6N45R10Y TEXT:"Reuters/Ipsos poll"]. That poll also showed registered voters preferring Democrats over Republicans nationally by 44% to 37%. Among independents, Democrats led 37% to 21%, with 28% of independent voters still undecided. Republicans hold a 53-47 majority in the US Senate, where Democrats must net four seats in the November 3 midterm elections to control the chamber — an already difficult task that makes Cooper's North Carolina race especially important. Cooper's signature bipartisan achievement did not come easily. It took him six years to persuade the Republican-controlled state legislature to pass an expansion of Medicaid under Obamacare in 2023, extending health insurance to more than 700,000 state residents, according to state health department data. After passage, he called it “an unnecessarily long and agonizing journey.” Whit Ayres, a Republican pollster, said several moderate Democratic governors in the South could replicate Cooper’s success, including Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear. “The Roy Coopers of the world are not unique,” Ayres said. “The Republicans nominated someone who’s never been elected to any public office at any level anywhere running against a reasonably moderate, popular governor.” RUNNING AGAINST HEALTHCARE CUTS Many of the state’s Medicaid gains are likely to be undone by Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill,” a sweeping tax and budget bill the Republican-led Congress passed last year that cuts about $1 trillion from Medicaid, the largest cut in the program’s history, according to the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office. Cooper has used Trump’s signature domestic legislative achievement to paint the president and Republicans as depriving North Carolinians of healthcare in order to give billionaires more tax cuts. He has also focused on congressional Republicans’ decision to curtail COVID-era Obamacare subsidies last year, causing healthcare premiums on the individual health insurance marketplace to spike and more than 200,000 state residents to drop their coverage, according to health policy research firm KFF. “Roy Cooper has always polled over Republicans,” said Anderson Clayton, chair of the North Carolina Democratic Party. “This will be the average election for Roy Cooper.”

item.title: Microsoft pulls out of UK data center deal with Nscale, Telegraph reports
item.description: Microsoft has pulled out of a data center deal with British cloud provider Nscale, Britain's Telegraph newspaper reported on Sunday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Microsoft (MSFT.O) has pulled out of a data center deal with British cloud provider Nscale, Britain's Telegraph newspaper reported on Sunday. The US tech giant, one of Nscale's two largest customers, recently terminated its agreement for the data center in Loughton, Essex, according to the report. The newspaper did not specify why Microsoft withdrew from the project. Microsoft declined a Reuters request for comment. The Telegraph report said Nscale had faced repeated delays with the project. National power grid officials, it reported, had told Nscale they did not expect a power supply for the data center until the 2030s. "Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term, and this unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts," an Nscale spokesperson told Reuters. "We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK, and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK." Nscale filed for an [USN:L4N45A197 TEXT:"initial public offering"] in the US last month, with Microsoft and Anthropic expected to be its major customers, according to its prospectus. Nscale [USN:L4N45A1JP TEXT:"provides"] infrastructure, including compute, power and data centers, as well as software for training and running AI models. The Nvidia-backed (NVDA.O) AI group, which competes against CoreWeave (CRWV.O) , Nebius (NBIS.O) , Crusoe and Lambda, has grown rapidly since its launch, scaling from $100 million to more than $103 billion in total contracted value in just two-and-a-half years.

item.title: Carney’s pipeline push is unlikely to bring back Canada’s oil jobs boom
item.description: Even Mark Carney won’t call it a boom. While Canada’s oil output may rise, experts don’t expect to see major job creation.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Stephenson
item.content:encoded: A Syncrude oil sands plant outside the Alberta oil hub of Fort McMurray, seen from a helicopter. Alberta's oil sands contain one of the world's largest unconventional petroleum reserves in a thick, sticky form of oil called bitumen. Canada's Prime Minister, Mark Carney, wants to export more oil to Asia to blunt the impact of President Donald Trump's tariffs. REUTERS/Todd Korol Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney is betting a new pipeline can help revive the country’s oil industry, boost its production and exports, and reduce its dependence on the United States. Bringing back jobs will be much harder. In the Alberta oil hub of Fort McMurray – nicknamed Fort McMoney in its heyday more than a decade ago – the tens of thousands of oil field jobs that powered the last boom are unlikely to return, even if Carney gets his pipeline. Instead, much of the growth in oil sands output is likely to come from automation and efficiency gains rather than large-scale hiring, according to industry forecasts and nearly a dozen interviews with company officials, workers, politicians and academics. The pipeline backed by Carney would transport 1 million barrels of crude oil a day to a port on the Pacific coast, expanding export capacity to Asia. Asked by Reuters what the pipeline would mean for the region’s economy, Carney – a former central banker – cautioned against anticipating a return to the oil-boom days. "I wouldn't use the term 'boom'," Carney said during a visit to Fort McMurray this month. "I would use ‘sustained growth’." A giant dump truck hauls unprocessed oil at a Suncor mine near Fort McMurray, Alberta. REUTERS/Todd Korol A construction worker on the job at a new commercial building in the Alberta oil sands hub of Fort McMurray. REUTERS/Todd Korol MORE OIL, FEWER WORKERS More oil without many more permanent jobs could leave Carney politically exposed on two fronts: Critics on the left say his efforts to fast-track the project’s regulatory approval risks sacrificing the environment, while those on the right argue the deregulation should deliver faster economic growth, higher salaries and more oil jobs. Low job growth could also further fuel Alberta’s separatist movement, though a referendum on whether to hold a vote to leave Canada is expected to fail on Monday. An August labor forecast by industry group Energy Safety Canada projects that oil sands employment will fall by 920 jobs or 4% by 2035, even as production grows 6%. A spokesperson for Energy Safety Canada told Reuters that a new West Coast pipeline would likely reverse the projected job decline but may not add many permanent jobs because of the “structural trend” of producing more oil with fewer workers. "Nobody should expect that something that happened 15 years ago will happen the same way today," said Dianna De Sousa, CEO of the Fort McMurray Chamber of Commerce. A spokesperson for Carney declined to comment on the lackluster projections for job creation from the pipeline, referring questions to the Department of Natural Resources, which did not respond. FROM BOOM TO BUST TO WILDFIRES From 2000 to 2014, Canadian and international oil companies spent billions to build out the mega-mines and other facilities required to extract bitumen, the thick oil found in northern Alberta. Fort McMurray became a place where workers fresh out of high school could earn six-figure salaries, putting new pickups and pricey boats in their driveways. A boarded-up hotel for sale offers a reminder of the downturn in Fort McMurray's fortunes. REUTERS/Todd Korol Colorful trees grow in a burnt-out forest outside Fort McMurray. REUTERS/Todd Korol A new community of houses in Fort McMurray. Housing values have declined sharply over the last decade. REUTERS/Todd Korol Rush-hour traffic on a major downtown street in Fort McMurray. REUTERS/Todd Korol A delivery driver walks to a store in downtown Fort McMurray. REUTERS/Todd Korol Sarah Thapa, owner of Avenue Eatery and Cafe in Fort McMurray. REUTERS/Todd Korol Guests look at a display in the local Oil Sands Museum. REUTERS/Todd Korol Fly-in, fly-out workers — some from as far as 5,000 km (3,107 miles) away – packed on-site work camps because the city lacked housing. Then came the 2015 oil price crash, followed by a devastating wildfire one year later. Investors’ growing focus on environmental, social and governance (ESG) criteria combined with the climate policies of Carney's predecessor Justin Trudeau deepened the slump. Nobody should expect that something that happened 15 years ago will happen the same way today. Dianna De Sousa, CEO of the Fort McMurray Chamber of Commerce International oil majors exited. Annual oil sands capital investment fell from a C35billion(24.55 billion) peak in 2014 to C$14.2 billion in 2024, according to Statistics Canada. The last major new oil sands project, Suncor's Fort Hills, started up in 2018. Alberta’s oil and gas sector employs 435,000 people today, including temporary and part-time workers, 85,000 fewer than in 2014, according to data from Alberta’s Servus Credit Union. Real disposable income in the province is still 10% below 2014 levels. Housing values have declined sharply. Stronger oil prices and rising production have brought some signs of recovery, including regional population growth for the first time in a decade. But flights from Calgary and other major cities sometimes arrive nearly empty, and vacant commercial spaces dot downtown. "Things are not getting better," said Jenny Parsons, who has worked as a truck driver and contractor at oil sands sites since moving from Newfoundland 15 years ago. She said she was earning barely a dollar more an hour than she was in 2011. Jenny Parsons says her wages have flatlined since the boom collapsed over a decade ago. She will vote yes on Monday to holding a referendum on Alberta separation. REUTERS/Todd Korol WHAT A PIPELINE COULD BRING No oil sands company has committed the C$100 billion in private investment needed to fill the proposed pipeline and build the carbon capture and storage project Carney has made a condition of federal approval. Kendall Dilling, head of the Oil Sands Alliance, which represents the five largest companies, said the projects could create thousands of jobs across Canada by the mid-2030s, including upstream investment and supply-chain activity as well as pipeline construction. But many of these jobs would be temporary construction jobs, in British Columbia as well as Alberta, rather than permanent oil-industry jobs. Some of those jobs no longer exist. Efficiency gains, for example, have cut the time oil companies spend on routine maintenance, which has reduced the number of staff as well as contract positions, he said. The employment gains “may be less than the absolute peaks that we've seen in the past.” Jason Kenney, Alberta's conservative premier from 2019 to 2022, cut corporate taxes to get oil sands companies to spend on big projects. But even after oil prices rose and revenue stabilized, companies prioritized shareholder returns over job growth, he told Reuters. "I was certainly frustrated with them,” he told Reuters. He said he urged companies to allocate some of the tax cut savings to their capital plans. "The people need to see a benefit, not just the shareholder in New York." A Suncor oil sands mine outside Fort McMurray. The company launched the last major new oil sands project in the area in 2018. REUTERS/Todd Korol The industry group representing oil companies did not respond directly to Kenney's comments but said the pipeline provided an opportunity to increase production, create jobs and grow government revenue. CARNEY FACES RISKS FROM LEFT AND RIGHT By backing a new pipeline, Carney — who grew up in Alberta's capital of Edmonton — has brokered an uneasy truce between the federal government and Alberta conservatives. But he has angered some in his own Liberal party by embracing oil to help the Canadian economy survive President Donald Trump’s tariffs. He has repealed many of Trudeau's environmental policies, cut the tax rate on new capital investment, and is promoting Canadian oil to investors abroad. While Carney’s approval rating was at 62% in a September poll from Angus Reid, public sentiment on energy and the environment can shift quickly. "It's important to remember that the environmental policies of Justin Trudeau were widely popular at the time," said Lori Williams, a political science professor at Calgary’s Mount Royal University. "If we see more environmentally friendly options starting to come on in the future then I think additional pipelines in Canada will be much harder to sell." Fort McMurray's boom had its downsides. The flood of workers strained local infrastructure and created tensions between locals and the thousands of people in work camps. Some oil sands companies now hire more locals to reduce their reliance on fly-in workers, a shift that reflects a leaner but steadier industry. Still, longtime residents like Colin Hartigan, owner of the city’s Coldwell Banker United office, hope that Carney's ambitions will bring back at least an echo of the old Fort McMurray. "At some point, there's going to be another boom," Hartigan said. "Do I think families here want to see that? Not like in the past, that was a little bit crazy. But do we all pray for it? Absolutely." The Suncor oil sands mine outside Fort McMurray. The company is one of the major producers in the oil patch. REUTERS/Todd Korol

item.title: France counts the cost of worst unrest in years as tensions flare again in Paris
item.description: Police fired tear gas toward protesters at Place de la République and bikes were set on fire on Sunday, a day after nationwide demonstrations erupted into the worst unrest France has seen in years.
item.dc:creator: Sybille de La Hamaide
item.content:encoded: Fresh clashes broke out in Paris on Sunday a day after France suffered one of its worst days of unrest in years, with protests over high prices leaving one demonstrator dead, thousands arrested and shops across the country looted or damaged. Nationwide demonstrations erupted into riots on Saturday, with a town hall torched, shops ransacked, and buildings covered in graffiti as violent groups clashed with police in cities across the country. One protester died after suffering a cardiac arrest during [USN:L1N46302B TEXT:"demonstrations"] in Paris. Police made more than 2,000 arrests across France, while more than 600 officers were injured, the interior minister said. "It's like a war zone here," said Dutch entrepreneur Tije De Boer, who had come to Paris with his children to visit a friend and said the protests forced him to evacuate his hotel at Place de la Republique, a trouble hotspot on Saturday. Police again clashed with protesters and fired tear gas at Place de la Republique on Sunday afternoon, and packs of bikes were set on fire. A Reuters witness estimated several hundred protesters were in the area. In Marseille, France's second largest city, the local prefecture also reported some incidents in the afternoon, with attempts made by groups to break into shops. More than half a million people joined marches in scores of cities on Saturday, marking the convergence of a month-long [USN:L6N45M1EJ TEXT:"student movement"] with broader social discontent against rising living costs and declining public services. President Emmanuel Macron will address the nation at 8 p.m. local time (1800 GMT) on Sunday, his office said. Saturday's unrest laid bare the deep anger at Macron, who leaves office in 2027 after a decade in power that has increasingly become defined by social discontent, a weak economy and ballooning debt. The government has blamed the violence on hard-left and ultra-left groups, as well as criminals who it said instigated the looting. French far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen called for calm, saying France must not become accustomed to images of the country being battered, abused, and ransacked. "Violence is not an opinion. Destruction is not a form of expression. And chaos cannot serve as a project for France," she said in a video address. SEVERAL HUNDRED SHOPS DAMAGED While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, looted luxury boutiques and supermarkets, and attacked police vehicles and officers. A massive clean-up operation began in cities from Lille in the north to Marseille in the south and Strasbourg in the east to Bordeaux in the southwest, where a masked mob invaded the residence of the local prefect. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said several hundred shops had been damaged on Saturday. In [USN:L1N46402C TEXT:"Limoges"], southwestern France, Mayor Guillaume Guerin denounced the chaos after the city's 143-year-old town hall was set ablaze and largely destroyed in an arson attack on Saturday, drawing comparisons to the 2019 fire that devastated Paris's Notre-Dame Cathedral. "There was a clear, premeditated intention to burn down the town hall, and the people inside feared for their lives," Guerin told Reuters. He threatened to resign if the city did not receive the funds needed to repair the town hall. PRESIDENTIAL ELECTION TO TAKE PLACE NEXT YEAR The unrest has increased pressure on President Macron and his government ahead of a presidential election due next year. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu blamed the unrest on the "ultra-left" and criminals. Economy Minister Roland Lescure pledged support on Sunday for business owners who suffered losses. "Those who break things will pay, repair the damage and be held accountable for their intention to sow chaos," Lescure said in a statement. Bordeaux Mayor Thomas Cazenave said up to 100 stores had been looted in his city, while Marseille Mayor Benoit Payan announced emergency financial aid to support those businesses impacted by the violence. French retailer Carrefour's (CARR.PA) CEO Alexandre Bompard told French broadcaster BFMTV that 50 of the company's shops had been damaged, including 20 that were looted, with losses from the damage running into the tens of millions of euros. The protests began last month over school conditions and teacher shortages in working-class suburbs, before broadening into a movement against inequality, public spending cuts and the rising cost of living.

item.title: Japan PM Takaichi's support rate falls below 50%, lowest since taking office, Kyodo reports
item.description: The approval rating for Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's administration fell below 50% to its lowest level since she took office in October last year, Kyodo News Agency reported on Sunday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The approval rating for Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's administration fell below 50% to its lowest level since she took office in October last year, Kyodo News Agency reported on Sunday. In a poll conducted between October 17 and 18, the approval rating for Takaichi's administration was 49.1%, the report said. The decline might have been affected by Takaichi's slow response surrounding the resignation of Kazuo Yana as the nation's farm minister, the report said. Yana [USN:L6N4600KT TEXT:"stepped down"] from the post on Wednesday after coming under fire for remarks about cutting road funding for municipalities that did not support him. Some 57.7% of respondents said Takaichi's decision to replace him came "too late," Kyodo said, while 81.5% said it was natural for Yana to resign. Takaichi appointed Yana in a cabinet reshuffle last month, but had openly chided him in parliament for the remarks over the road funding, which local media first reported earlier this month.

item.title: Australia's Smith says head blow left him anxious in first test concussion scare
item.description: Australia batsman Steve Smith said he was anxious after being hit on the head and facing the prospect of another concussion after a blow playing against South Africa in the first test a week ago.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Australia batsman Steve Smith said he was anxious after being hit on the head and facing the prospect of another concussion after a blow playing against South Africa in the first test a week ago. Former captain Smith has previously suffered multiple concussions in his career, and he had to go through concussion protocols after a bouncer from Anrich Nortje hit him on the helmet last Monday during the second-last day of the clash at Kingsmead in Durban. “I was a little bit anxious after the hit, to be honest,” Smith said on Sunday before the start of the second test at St George’s Park in a television interview. “It was a decent knock, and the rest of that day, I wasn't travelling too well, and I think it was more to do with anxiety, of hoping not to feel what I felt in the past, waking up the next morning and things like that. “So, yeah, fortunately, I woke up well. I passed all the tests, and things recovered pretty quickly,” Smith added as he prepared to take part in the rain-delayed second test. The 37-year-old was assessed on the field by the physio and the doctor, and his helmet was changed as is mandatory for all such hits, but he continued his innings, scoring 27 runs as Australia built a large lead. PASSED CONCUSSION PROTOCOLS But then Smith did not take to the field at the start of South Africa's second innings on Monday, instead being subjected to the concussion protocols, which he passed. He returned from the start of the last day’s play on Tuesday to help his side to a 214-run victory and a 1-0 lead in the three-match series. Smith, who is 28 short of 11,000 test runs, was the first player replaced in a test after the introduction of a concussion substitute. He was struck on the back of the head by a Jofra Archer bouncer in the 2019 Ashes test at Lord's in London. He also suffered a concussion after being hit on the head in practice during Australia's One Day International series in England in 2020 and two months later, back home in Sydney, woke on the morning of the second ODI against India with vertigo and was sick. There have also been incidents in Sri Lanka in 2022, at the last World Cup in India and last December in the Ashes at Adelaide where he was ruled out of the third test about 20 minutes before the toss with a vestibular issue, the sensory system located in the inner ear that controls balance and spatial orientation.

item.title: Congo confirms Ebola outbreak has spread to eighth province
item.description: The Ebola outbreak in Democratic Republic of Congo has spread to an eighth province, North Ubangi, Congo's public health institute said on Sunday, confirming earlier Reuters reporting.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The Ebola outbreak in Democratic Republic of Congo has spread to an eighth province, North Ubangi, Congo's public health institute said on Sunday, confirming earlier Reuters reporting. The emergence of cases in the province, which borders Central African Republic, poses a new challenge for health authorities struggling to contain the outbreak. The National Institute for Biomedical Research confirmed two cases - including one death - in North Ubangi. Reuters [USN:L6N461199 TEXT:"reported on Thursday"] that two cases were confirmed in the province, citing two health officials. At the time, there was no official statement by Congolese authorities. North Ubangi becomes the eighth province affected by the outbreak, alongside North Kivu, Ituri, Haut-Uele, Tshopo, Sud-Kivu, Bas-Uele and South Ubangi. The outbreak, the worst Ebola epidemic in Congo's history, has already spread beyond the country's borders, with cases recorded in Uganda and seven infections [USN:L8N4621HW TEXT:"confirmed in Kenya"] this month. Congo's latest situation report showed 67 new confirmed cases and 26 new deaths in the 24 hours to Oct.16, bringing the cumulative total to 9,415 cases and 4,536 deaths since the outbreak began. The outbreak remains concentrated in eastern Congo, with Ituri province reporting 44 of the 67 new cases.
