item.title: Macron dénonce la "violence débridée" et appelle à la responsabilité
item.description: Emmanuel Macron a dénoncé une "violence débridée" qu'il a imputée à des "factieux" d'ultra-gauche et à des délinquants au lendemain des scènes de violence et de pillages qui ont terni une journée de vaste mobilisation contre la vie chère dans toute la France.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Emmanuel Macron a dénoncé une "violence débridée" qu'il a imputée à des "factieux" d'ultra-gauche et à des délinquants au lendemain des scènes de violence et de pillages qui ont terni une journée de vaste mobilisation contre la vie chère dans toute la France. Dans une allocution solennelle diffusée à la télévision au moment où Paris connaissait de nouvelles scènes de chaos, le chef de l'Etat a promis des aides rapides aux commerçants dont les magasins ont été pillés, affirmé que "ceux qui ont détruit doivent payer" et renvoyé sur les préfets et les maires la responsabilité d'interdire de futurs rassemblements. Appelant l'ensemble des partis politiques à faire preuve de responsabilité à sept mois de l'élection présidentielle, il a aussi promis de répondre aux "revendications légitimes" des manifestants, notamment celles des lycéens et des étudiants. Initialement né sur les réseaux sociaux, l'appel à manifester le 17 octobre avait été relayé par les syndicats lycéens qui se mobilisent depuis la mi-septembre pour obtenir de meilleures conditions d'enseignement, ainsi que par des organisations syndicales. Le ministère de l'Intérieur a dénombré 550.000 manifestants dans tout le pays, dont 110.000 à Paris, la CGT faisant état pour sa part de 800.000 personnes dans les cortèges, qui se sont dans l'ensemble déroulés sans incident. PRINCIPAUX DÉVELOPPEMENTS : 20h10 - Le président Emmanuel Macron dénonce la "violence débridée de factieux de la mouvance d'ultra-gauche et de délinquants", disant avoir éprouvé de la "honte" face à l'ampleur des dégradations. Dans une allocution solennelle, le chef de l'Etat a promis des aides aux commerçants victimes de pillages et renvoyé sur les préfets la responsabilité de "protéger nos villes, nos bâtiments publics et nos commerces", si besoin en interdisant certains rassemblements qui pourraient dégénérer. Prônant le dialogue avec les manifestants qui ont exprimé pacifiquement des revendications "légitimes", il a assuré que les autorités se montreraient "intraitables" avec les casseurs. "L'écoute et le dialogue ne signifient ni la faiblesse ni l'impunité", a-t-il dit. Emmanuel Macron a enfin demandé à l'ensemble des partis politiques et des syndicats de condamner les violences et d'appeler au calme pour permettre à la campagne de l'élection présidentielle de se dérouler dans les meilleures conditions. "Le pays a besoin d'ordre et d'apaisement", a-t-il plaidé. 18h20 - "La République, ce n'est pas le pillage", déclare Edouard Philippe, ancien Premier ministre d'Emmanuel Macron et candidat à l'élection présidentielle, en pointant du doigt la responsabilité de "l'ultra-gauche" dans les violences qui émaillent les mouvements sociaux. 18h00 - "Notre pays est pris en étau, voire en otage, entre la violence et l'impuissance", déclare Marine Le Pen dans une allocution aux Français. "Ce qui se joue aujourd'hui dépasse cette question de l'ordre public, nous vivons une crise profonde de confiance, d'autorité qui fait peser une menace sur la démocratie", ajoute la candidate du Rassemblement national en vue de la prochaine élection présidentielle. "Ces événements violents ne sont pas nés de rien, ils interviennent dans un contexte délétère que le gouvernement a lui même créé (...) Les inquiétudes, les souffrances, les plaintes des Français se sont transformées en exaspération et même parfois en colère. Ces colères sont souvent légitimes tant les crises se sont succédé sans qu'aucune décision ne soit prise, mais que les choses soient claires, très claires : il y a des millions de Français qui sont en colère mais qui ne cassent rien, qui ne pillent rien, ne brûlent rien. Je condamne ainsi fermement l'instrumentalisation de ces colères par des forces politiques qui encouragent la violence." 17h10 - "La France a été humiliée", déclare le président du Rassemblement national (RN), Jordan Bardella, à propos des violences qui ont émaillé la journée de samedi. "Que Macron s'en aille, demande pardon", ajoute le dirigeant d'extrême droite, dénonçant un dispositif de maintien de l'ordre "manifestement sous-dimensionné". 17h00 - De nouveaux heurts entre la police et des émeutiers ont lieu autour de la place de la République à Paris, montrent les images diffusées par les chaînes d'information en continu. 14h30 - Le ministre de l'Intérieur, Laurent Nuñez, annonce sur X un nouveau bilan de plus de 2.000 personnes interpellées et de plus de 600 policiers, gendarmes et pompiers blessés. 12h55 - Dans un communiqué, la Confédération des commerçants de France, qui dit représenter plus de 7.000 TPE du commerce et de l'artisanat dans les centre-villes, estime que près de 1.500 commerces ont été touchés à travers la France samedi. 12h45 - Emmanuel Macron réunira à 17h30 à l'Elysée le Premier ministre Sébastien Lecornu et les ministres du gouvernement concernés et s'adressera solennellement aux Français à 20h00, annonce l'Elysée. 11h35 - "Je veux des explications et des moyens pour que cela ne se reproduise plus", déclare à la presse le maire socialiste de Marseille, Benoît Payan, alors que le ministre de l'Intérieur est attendu lundi dans la ville. "Mon propos n'est pas d'incriminer la police nationale. La police nationale, elle fait en fonction de qu'on lui demande (...). Je veux savoir quels ordres leurs ont été donnés, je veux savoir s'il leur a été demandé de s'occuper uniquement des manifestants et de lancer des lacrymos sur les manifestants et de ne pas s'occuper des pillages dans la ville." 11h20 - "Pendant une heure, je n'ai pas eu un seul policier national pour protéger la mairie", déclare sur BFM TV Guillaume Guérin, maire LR de Limoges. "On a un problème de soutien de nos forces de l'ordre", ajoute-t-il en déclarant avoir été informé par des policiers qu'ils manquaient de munitions. 11h00 - Le ministre de l'Intérieur, Laurent Nuñez, annonce sur X un bilan de 1.800 personnes interpellées samedi en France et de plus de 500 policiers, gendarmes et pompiers blessés. 10h45 - La secrétaire nationale des Ecologistes Marine Tondelier réclame sur X la démission du ministre de l'Intérieur Laurent Nuñez, "manifestement dépassé par la situation". 10h12 - "Ce bilan est désastreux car il emporte de lourdes conséquences : d’abord sur les libertés et notamment celle de manifester puisqu’elle est entravée par la violence ; ensuite sur la jeunesse confrontée à la brutalité et privée des réponses attendues du Gouvernement ; enfin sur l’État qui n’a pas été capable d’assurer partout l’ordre public", estime l'ancien président François Hollande dans un message sur X. 09h45 - A Lyon, le préfet du Rhône, Etienne Guyot, fait état de 160 personnes interpellées et placées en garde à vue et d'une centaine de membres des forces de l'ordre blessés. 08h50 - "Nous avons une ville dans une situation de délabrement total", déplore sur franceinfo la première adjointe au maire de Paris, Lamia El Araaje. "Nous avons assisté à des scènes de pillage méthodiques qui n'ont rien à voir avec les revendications sociales." "A l'évidence, les forces de l'ordre ont été débordées (...) Il y a eu clairement un manque de moyens", dit-elle. 08h15 - Une personne est décédée à la suite d'un arrêt cardiorespiratoire samedi à Paris lors des manifestations contre la vie chère, pendant lesquelles 855 interpellations ont été effectuées, ce qui représente un "chiffre record", déclare la préfecture de police dans un bilan établi à 08h00. Treize policiers et gendarmes et deux sapeurs-pompiers ont été blessés, ajoute-t-elle.

item.title: Boland strikes twice on rain-hit first day
item.description: Australia bowler Scott Boland took two wickets in as many balls to leave South Africa 20 runs for two wickets at the close of play on a rain-hampered first day of the second test at St George’s Park on Sunday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Australia bowler Scott Boland took two wickets in as many balls to leave South Africa 20 runs for two wickets at the close of play on a rain-hampered first day of the second test at St George’s Park on Sunday. Boland, who was the only change in the Australia team after their first 214-run test victory in Durban, bowled opener Aiden Markram for 11 and snagged David Bedingham for a duck with his next delivery as the South African batsman feathered the ball into wicketkeeper Alex Carey’s gloves. Debutant Marques Ackerman was five not out and captain Temba Bavuma on four when rain stopped play some 40 minutes after lunch and did not abate, leading to stumps being called one hour and 45 minutes before the scheduled close. A total of one hour’s play was possible after Australia won the toss and put South Africa into bat. The toss went ahead as scheduled but as soon as it was completed the covers came on again, after overnight rain, and play did not begin until two hours after the scheduled start. South Africa were 11–0 when rain stopped play and early lunch was called, returning for a half hour after lunch during which Boland struck. In his first test appearance in South Africa, the accurate seamer got the ball to nip in and induce an inside edge from Markram for his first wicket. His next ball seamed away, tempting Bedingham into a nick and dismissing him for a golden duck. Ackerman, making his test debut aged 30, was opening in a first-class game for the first time and despite obvious nerves, was circumspect in his shot selection against the Australian opening bowlers on a green top. The test sees a return for South Africa’s top paceman Kagiso Rabada, who has not played cricket since the Indian Premier League in May, and hurt his hamstring in off-season training. Rabada replaced spinner Keshav Maharaj and Matthew Breetzke won a recall in the middle order as Tristan Stubbs was dropped.

item.title: German police investigate fence breach at Leipzig airport
item.description: German police were investigating a breach at the Leipzig/Halle airport after a vehicle appeared to have broken through a fence and driven a few metres before exiting, a Leipzig police spokesperson said on Sunday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: German police were investigating a breach at the Leipzig/Halle airport after a vehicle appeared to have broken through a fence and driven a few metres before exiting, a Leipzig police spokesperson said on Sunday. The spokesperson, briefing journalists after police spent the day searching the scene, said authorities had not yet found the vehicle and were still trying to determine whether the breach was an accident or a crime In August, investigators discovered [USN:L8N4420RI TEXT:"an explosive-laden drone"] near a runway at the airport, an event that German officials later said [USN:L8N44T1P2 TEXT:"Russia was responsible"] for. Russia has denied the allegations One runway had been closed but was again operating, the police spokesperson said German police first responded to the breach late on Saturday evening Leipzig police said they had not found suspicious objects or unauthorized people Officers on Sunday could be seen inspecting the area around a large break in the chain-link and barbed-wire fence

item.title: Lithuanians forced to take shelter after suspected drone enters airspace
item.description: Ukraine's foreign ministry said the incident may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare diverting its drones off course.
item.dc:creator: Andrius Sytas
item.content:encoded: A suspected drone exploded over Lithuania after triggering an alert that forced residents in northern and central areas to seek shelter for an hour on Sunday morning, the president and other defence officials said. Ukraine 's Foreign Ministry [USN:L8N46404Q TEXT:"said"] later it regretted the incident in Lithuania's airspace, adding that it may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare diverting drones off course. The object flew into Lithuania's airspace from Poland, Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas told reporters, after proposing a joint investigation to his Polish counterpart. "Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine is spilling over onto the Eastern flank of NATO and EU," Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda said on X. "What appears to be a drone exploded over the northern part of the country, posing a danger to the civilian population," he added. NATO SCRAMBLES FIGHTERS Poland's military said it was also [USN:FWN4630JH TEXT:"verifying a possible violation of its airspace"] by an unidentified object. A Polish Defence Ministry spokesperson later said radar systems did not confirm the object crossing the border into Lithuania, but added that Polish authorities were remaining in contact with Lithuanian officials. During the "red" alert, NATO fighter jets were scrambled to the area, and Kaunas airport, near Lithuania's second-largest city, was temporarily closed, the Lithuanian government's crisis management centre said. The NATO aircraft were unable to visually identify the object due to cloudy weather and did not attempt to shoot it down, the centre said. Lithuanian army personnel were investigating possible drone debris near Juodzionys village in northern Lithuania, after the object disappeared from radar, possibly after exploding, the centre said. Some of the debris struck a civilian vehicle, Kaunas said. "We can confirm that two Italian Eurofighter jets were scrambled earlier today in response to a drone over Lithuanian airspace," a NATO official said. "The aircraft were operating under NATO command. An investigation is ongoing, and NATO remains in close contact with the Lithuanian authorities," the official said, adding that the alliance was ready and able to react to any potential threat. Northern neighbour Latvia briefly issued a "yellow" air warning in some regions bordering Lithuania, citing a "possible threat", its army said. Ukrainian drones have repeatedly [USN:L8N41X1AC TEXT:"entered NATO airspace"] in the Baltic region in recent months. Kyiv has said they were steered off course by Russian signal jamming. This has stoked concerns that Russia's war in Ukraine is spilling over NATO's borders.

item.title: Rubio arrives in Central Asia while other US officials hit foreign policy hot spots
item.description: While the Iran war smolders, Saudi Arabia fights the Houthis and a new rift opens in US-Ukraine relations, Secretary of State Marco Rubio traveled on Sunday to Uzbekistan, a nation far removed from the biggest US foreign policy challenges.
item.dc:creator: Gram Slattery, Simon Lewis
item.content:encoded: While the Iran war smolders, Saudi Arabia fights the Houthis and a new rift opens in US-Ukraine relations, Secretary of State Marco Rubio traveled on Sunday to Uzbekistan, a nation far removed from the biggest US foreign policy challenges. The top US diplomat landed in Samarkand on Sunday night to meet with top officials from the C5+1, a grouping that brings together the United States and the Muslim-majority post-Soviet states of Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan. US officials have portrayed resource-rich Central Asia — the region between China, Russia and Iran — as worthy of more attention than it received from US President Donald Trump's predecessors. Trump hosted C5 leaders at the White House last November, when Kazakhstan agreed to join the Abraham Accords, a series of agreements under which Muslim-majority countries have normalized or deepened relations with Israel. Separately, Trump met with Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev at the United Nations General Assembly in September of last year. Regional politics aside, the trip fits an emerging pattern in which Rubio often visits regions not at the center of the news cycle, while leaving some more fraught foreign policy portfolios to other Trump aides, including special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and Vice President JD Vance. Rubio has not visited Kyiv or Moscow since becoming secretary of state and was not present for talks between US and Ukrainian officials in Florida earlier this month, when US officials pressed Ukraine to stop hitting Russian refineries. Vance, not Rubio, represented the US in Pakistan during peace talks with Iran in April. Rubio's previous foreign trip, in early October, took him to Greece, Portugal and Iceland. Trump administration officials have typically rejected any suggestion that cabinet-level officials should focus their travels on geopolitical capitals and hot spots. Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau, for instance, said on X last week that the idea only certain destinations were worthy of visits from secretaries of state "perfectly encapsulates the decadence and degeneracy of the contemporary US foreign policy establishment." Speaking to reporters before leaving Washington on Saturday, Rubio said the timing of the Uzbekistan trip was dictated in part by the availability of the various delegations. He also said that foreign trips were too often designed to resolve immediate issues rather than build long-term relationships. "I mean, one of the things that suffers is the strategic business," Rubio told reporters. "You're always visiting someplace where there's a crisis or there's a problem or ... you're going because there's a conference." US-RUSSIA RELATIONS LOOM The delegation that greeted Rubio upon his arrival in Samarkand included Uzbek Foreign Minister Bakhtiyor Saidov, whom Rubio embraced warmly. Two women in traditional Uzbek attire presented Rubio and his wife with bouquets. One Central Asian diplomat, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said officials in the region were wondering to what extent the US would continue targeting Russian sanctions evasion. All C5 states, while drawing closer to the US, have deep historical ties with Moscow, and the region has facilitated Russian imports and exports that violate US and European Union sanctions, Western officials say. In the past, the US has pushed regional states to clamp down on those illicit flows. But Trump struck a deal with Moscow this month to [USN:L1N45Y0GJ TEXT:"import Russian diesel"], aimed at lowering domestic fuel prices before congressional midterm elections. On Friday, Trump [USN:L1N463009 TEXT:"waived"] all provisions of legislation that would have allowed him to slap massive tariffs on some nations that buy significant amounts of Russian crude oil or otherwise help Moscow evade sanctions. Among the nations that could have been affected, experts have said, are India and Kazakhstan. India, which Rubio will visit after Uzbekistan, remains the world's No. 2 Russian crude importer after China, despite Trump saying in February that India had agreed to stop buying oil from Russia. Additional questions hang over a potential trade deal with India and an expansion of the Abraham Accords in Central Asia. A US official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, described the trade deal on Friday as "pretty much done," raising the possibility that an agreement could be announced during the Rubio trip. Separately, the US [USN:L1N3TQ0WH TEXT:"has talked to"] additional Central Asian nations about joining the Abraham Accords, Reuters reported last year, conversations that potentially could continue in Samarkand. More than 200 business executives are accompanying Rubio to Uzbekistan, the State Department said. The Central Asian diplomat said the Trump administration has focused its commercial efforts on expanding access to the area's rare earth mineral resources. After Uzbekistan, Rubio will visit the Indian cities of Mumbai and Jamnagar to meet with business leaders, including Reliance Industries (RELI.NS) Chairman Mukesh Ambani, who earned the Trump administration's favor earlier in the year by backing a new refinery in Texas. Rubio most recently visited India five months ago. The trip is due to wrap up on Thursday.

item.title: Rubio says Trump to take up to 60 days to weigh Russia sanctions
item.description: The waiver on sanctions against Russia comes just weeks before the midterms.
item.dc:creator: Nandita Bose, Gram Slattery
item.content:encoded: The day after waiving sanctions and tariffs related to Russian exports, US President Donald Trump said on Saturday he has yet to announce a final decision on the matter as Secretary of State Marco Rubio said officials want more time to evaluate the situation. Rubio said on Saturday that the president will use up to 60 days to assess the economic impact of Russia-related sanctions and tariffs that he waived a day earlier. "A lot of you don't know what my decision is yet, but we'll figure it out, and you'll figure it out," Trump told reporters at his Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida. The waiver comes just weeks before November's [TOPIC:"reuters:/world/us/elections/" TEXT:"midterm elections"], with Trump under pressure over high energy prices as war with Iran disrupts global oil supplies. Trump signed an executive order on Friday waiving key sanctions and tariffs under the law known as the Graham Act, which he signed last month at the urging of lawmakers who want to pressure Moscow over its war in Ukraine. The measures, including tariffs on Russian goods and penalties on countries buying Russian oil and gas, were due to take effect next week. Friday's order did not specify how long the waiver would last, but Rubio said Trump opted for a 60-day review. "I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy," Rubio told reporters before boarding a plane for a trip to Uzbekistan. Complicating matters is the Graham Act's call not only for sanctions on Russia but also for tariffs on goods from countries that import Russian energy supplies. Rubio pointed to India, an important US partner that has diversified its energy supplies but remains heavily dependent on Russian oil. Friday's executive order [USN:L1N463009 TEXT:"drew criticism"] from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, who warned it would embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin and prolong the war. Senator Darline Graham, a South Carolina Republican whose late brother Lindsey Graham championed the legislation that bears his name, said she disagreed with Trump's decision and planned to discuss it with him when he campaigns for her next week. "Personally, I would choose to keep the pressure on Russia," she told reporters on Saturday. "Because I don't trust Putin and I don't trust Russia." DIESEL SUPPLIES Rubio also defended a separate US agreement with Russia to increase diesel supplies to global markets, aimed at easing fuel prices that have climbed amid the war with Iran and disruptions to energy supplies. Under the agreement, Trump said Russia initially would supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to the United States, followed by shipments in November and beyond. "That diesel is going to be sold one way or the other," Rubio said. "The only difference is how much of it the United States was going to get." Rubio said the diesel deal and sanctions waiver reflected the challenge of managing conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine that have disrupted global energy supplies. "These conflicts around the world are starting to crash into each other," he said.

item.title: Saudi-led coalition says helicopter crash in Najran kills two crew members
item.description: A reconnaissance AH-6i helicopter crashed in the Najran region of Saudi Arabia, killing its two crew members, the Saudi-led coalition's spokesperson Major General Turki al-Maliki said in a statement on Sunday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: A reconnaissance AH-6i helicopter crashed in the Najran region of Saudi Arabia, killing its two crew members, the Saudi-led coalition's spokesperson Major General Turki al-Maliki said in a statement on Sunday. The helicopter crashed due to a technical malfunction in an area under the jurisdiction of the Saudi National Guard Ministry, the statement added. Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis released footage later on Sunday of what they said was a Saudi AH-6i helicopter being shot down by a missile while carrying out what they described as hostile activities near Najran. The footage did not clearly show the incident, and Reuters could not immediately verify the Houthis' claim. There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities. On Saturday, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said on X that the group had shot down a Saudi Apache helicopter near Najran. It was not clear if that referred to the same incident. Al-Maliki commented on Saree's post on Sunday with a photo of several Apaches lined up, saying: "You claim to have shot it down, but it will enter the battlefield soon." Separately, the Saudi civil defence said on Sunday that six people were injured after a projectile it said was fired by Houthis fell on a residential area in Najran. Najran has been hit by attacks from the Houthis in recent weeks as fighting between the coalition and the Yemen-based group escalated, with the [USN:L1N4620VJ TEXT:"Yemen conflict"] becoming another front in the US-led war with Iran .

item.title: Deaths confirmed after 'serious incident,' fire at Canada military base in Alberta
item.description: People were killed and injured in a serious incident that resulted in a fire on one of Canada's busiest military bases in Alberta, Defense Minister David McGuinty said on Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Stephenson
item.content:encoded: People were killed and injured in a serious incident that resulted in a fire on one of Canada's busiest military bases in Alberta, Defense Minister David McGuinty said on Saturday. "I'm saddened to share that there have been both fatalities and injuries as a result of an incident" at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, McGuinty told reporters in Ottawa. He did not say how many people were killed or injured, or what caused the "tragic" situation at the base in the east-central part of the province, about 210 km (130 miles) east of Edmonton. A major fire was still burning on Saturday evening, he said, adding: "I cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory." The Canadian military and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are investigating the incident, McGuinty said. Prime Minister Mark Carney posted on social media that the national government was "working closely with the Government of Alberta and local authorities." CFB Wainwright had 1,310 military and civilian personnel stationed there as of 2021, according to census data. The town of Wainwright, population about 6,600, is just north of the base. The municipality posted on social media that the fire had crossed the base fence into the nearby district but no evacuation orders had been issued. General Jennie Carignan, the chief of Canada's Defense Staff, said on social media that the Canadian forces are fully engaged with federal, provincial and local authorities. "Our priority remains the welfare of our members, their families and their community," she said. (This story has been corrected to add the dropped word 'not' in paragraph 3.)

item.title: US wants Israel to 'crack down' on settler violence in West Bank, Rubio says
item.description: "We're very disturbed by those images and what we're seeing," Marco Rubio said.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The United States wants Israel to do more to deter attacks committed by settlers in the West Bank, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday. "We're very disturbed by those images and what we're seeing," Rubio said. "We've asked the Israelis and continue to ask them to crack down on that stuff." His comments to reporters came after the widespread dissemination of video showing multiple individuals attacking Heidi Levine, an American photojournalist with the Washington Post. Levine was one of at least two people injured in the Friday incident, which took place as Israeli settlers [USN:L6N46304S TEXT:"attacked"] Palestinian civilians. European diplomats and a French mayor also were attacked in the occupied West Bank, Belgium's foreign minister said. The US State Department, Rubio said, has inquired about the event that included Levine's attack. Rubio, who spoke to reporters before boarding a flight to Uzbekistan, said he expects to hear back from the US Embassy in Jerusalem by Sunday. Israeli settlers in the West Bank have been involved in at least 170 attacks on Palestinians since September 27, around the start of the annual olive harvest, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli settlements monitoring group.

item.title: Hurricanes win 7th straight, defeat Jets
item.description: Nikolaj Ehlers scored the go-ahead power-play goal in the third period as the Carolina Hurricanes rallied for their seventh straight victory, defeating the host Winnipeg Jets 3-2 on Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: Nikolaj Ehlers scored the go-ahead power-play goal in the third period as the Carolina Hurricanes rallied for their seventh straight victory, defeating the host Winnipeg Jets 3-2 on Saturday. Ehlers put Carolina ahead 3-2 with a power-play slap shot from the high slot at 6:43 of the third period for his first of the season. Mark Jankowski and Jesperi Kotkaniemi also scored, and Shayne Gostisbehere had two assists for the Hurricanes. Pyotr Kochetkov made 21 saves and improved to 5-0-0 on the season. Mark Scheifele and Alex Iafallo scored for the Jets, who have lost two straight games and three of their last four. Clay Stevenson made 34 saves. The Jets outshot the Hurricanes 10-8 in the first period. Carolina didn't register its first shot on goal until the 5:26 mark. Scheifele put Winnipeg ahead 1-0 at 4:23 of the second period on a backhanded shot. It was also the Jets' first shot of the period and extended Scheifele's points streak to five games. Jankowski tied the game 1-1 at 8:19 when Logan Stankoven set him up for a wrist shot through traffic on the power play. Iafallo gave the Jets a 2-1 lead at 10:59 when Adam Lowry intercepted Kochetkov's attempt to play the puck behind the net and set him up for a tap-in. Kotkaniemi knotted the score back up 2-2 at 16:50 when he tipped in Gostisbehere's shot from the blue line. Overall, Carolina won 55.2% of the faceoffs, and they outpaced Winnipeg in takeaways 6-4. Most importantly, they put a lot more pressure on the net with 37 shots compared to the Jets' 23 attempts. The Jets have now lost back-to-back games; they suffered a 4-3 overtime loss to the Chicago Blackhawks on Thursday. They will travel to St. Louis to take on the Blues on Tuesday. Meanwhile, Carolina is scheduled to face the Calgary Flames on the road on Sunday. --Field Level Media

item.title: Festival crush in Indian city of Kolkata kills at least 17, local media say
item.description: A crush at a religious festival in the eastern Indian city of Kolkata killed at least 17 people and injured dozens, local media reported on Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: A crush at a religious festival in the eastern Indian city of Kolkata killed at least 17 people and injured dozens, local media reported on Saturday. Durga Puja, a multi-day annual Hindu festival in the state of West Bengal, draws huge crowds to temporary structures known as pandals that house idols of the goddess Durga. The incident occurred at the exit gate in Kolkata's Girish Park area after heavy rain led to overcrowding as large numbers of devotees attempted to leave the venue, local TV said. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's office, in a post on social media platform X, announced a compensation payment of 200,000 rupees ($2,106.15) for the next of kin of those who died and 50,000 rupees each for the injured. ($1 = 94.9600 Indian rupees)

item.title: Israeli settlers attack Palestinians, European diplomats in West Bank, Belgium says
item.description: French and Polish diplomats and Catholic representatives were among those attacked, Belgium's foreign minister said, a day after settlers beat a Washington Post photojournalist.
item.dc:creator: Ali Sawafta, Mohammed Torokman
item.content:encoded: Israeli settlers attacked Palestinian civilians, European diplomats and a French mayor in the occupied West Bank on Saturday, Belgium's foreign minister said, a day after settlers beat an [USN:L8N4620II TEXT:"American photojournalist"]. Maxime Prevot said Belgium's consul general to the Palestinians, French and Polish diplomats, and Catholic representatives were among those attacked. A Belgian vehicle was also damaged, he said. "As the occupying power, Israeli authorities must protect Palestinians, ensure the safety of diplomats and journalists, and bring those responsible to justice. Impunity for violent settlers must end," Prevot said in a statement posted on X. 'THROWN TO THE GROUND' Bernard Baudoux, mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in northern France, told Reuters he had been harvesting olives near the Palestinian Christian village of Taybeh in solidarity with the local community when he was "violently attacked" by masked settlers. "I was thrown to the ground," he said. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar condemned the attack, describing the perpetrators as Israeli rioters. He also suggested the diplomats should have coordinated their visit with the Israeli military. "Such coordination could have helped safeguard the visitors’ security," he said in a statement on X. Palestinian Vice President Hussein al-Sheikh condemned the attack, calling it a small example of the "daily terrorism" to which Palestinians are subjected. Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, have periodically condemned settler violence, while saying it is carried out by a small minority. Palestinians and human rights groups dispute that characterisation. ISRAELI POLICE OPEN INVESTIGATION Settler attacks on Palestinians in the West Bank have surged over the past three years. Journalists, activists and foreign observers have also been targeted. On Friday, dozens of masked settlers attacked Palestinians harvesting olives in the West Bank. Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine, a US citizen covering the harvest, was hospitalised after being assaulted by masked settlers. "Palestinians face this violence every day. Settlers also target journalists reporting on it and diplomats. Harvesting olives, reporting the news or carrying out diplomatic duties should never put anyone at risk of attack," Prevot said. Belgium, which has announced a ban on imports from Israeli settlements in the West Bank and the Golan Heights, will press for European Union sanctions "against those responsible for this violence and those who support them," he added. Polish Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maciej Wewior said on X that a convoy carrying diplomats, including Polish officials, had been attacked. The Polish diplomats were unharmed. "Attacks on members of the diplomatic corps are absolutely unacceptable," he said. Israeli police said they had opened an investigation into the incident. There was no immediate announcement of any arrests. Prosecutions of settlers accused of violent crimes against Palestinians in the West Bank are rare.

item.title: Trump faults aides as Republican midterm prospects dim
item.description: "What's really happening is a circular firing squad."
item.dc:creator: Nandita Bose, Bo Erickson, Steve Holland
item.content:encoded: President Donald Trump is blaming senior aides and political operatives for a faltering [TOPIC:"reuters:/world/us/elections/" TEXT:"midterm strategy"], questioning campaign spending, faulting redistricting and second-guessing candidate choices as Republicans fight to retain control of Congress, said three people familiar with internal discussions. Trump is not on the November 3 ballot but repeatedly tells supporters to pretend that he is, hoping to mobilize voters who might otherwise skip the election. He has embarked on a frenetic campaign schedule while largely avoiding acknowledging his own role in shaping the strategy and how his unpopularity is weighing on Republican candidates in competitive races. Much of the friction has centered on James Blair, the longtime aide who runs Trump's super PAC MAGA Inc., and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, who until now had largely escaped criticism. Trump has faulted Blair's handling of campaign funds, while some White House officials and allies have questioned Wiles' oversight of the political operation. As Trump questions why campaign spending has failed to improve Republican polling numbers, his advisers are also blaming one another. Wiles has pointed to Blair, while Blair has faulted the White House legislative affairs team, one of the people said. "What's really happening is a circular firing squad," the person said. Opinion polls suggest Democrats will win the House of Representatives, while the Senate remains too close to call. Losing the House would hamper Trump's legislative agenda in the final two years of his term and give Democrats subpoena power to investigate his administration. Trump defended Wiles on Friday, calling her "smart" and "tough" and saying she would remain in her job. "Susie is here, and she's going to be here for a long time," he said. White House spokesman Davis Ingle rejected the sources' characterization, saying they were "armchair experts peddling their baseless speculation." Wiles did not respond to a request for comment. TRUMP HAS LONG DISTANCED HIMSELF FROM POLITICAL SETBACKS Trump has long sought to distance himself from political setbacks. He refused to accept his defeat in the 2020 election and said ahead of the 2022 midterm results that he deserved "all the credit" if Republicans won but "should not be blamed at all" if they lost. More recently, he has reminded audiences that the president's party typically struggles in midterm elections. But Trump helped devise and drive some of the strategies he is now questioning, including the redistricting effort and candidate choices shaped by his personal loyalties or grievances. His approval rating is at the lowest point of his presidency, weighed down by voter concern over high prices and dissatisfaction with the Iran war. Trump's frustrations with his political team spilled into public view after Blair and Chris LaCivita, who co-managed Trump's 2024 campaign, traveled in early October to Republika Srpska, a self-governing region of Bosnia. The New York Times reported the men received substantial payments to advise the regional government ahead of local elections. Trump distanced himself from both men, describing them as "outside consultants" in an October 7 Truth Social post and warning that if he found a conflict of interest, he would "terminate them, immediately!" Senior White House officials questioned why Blair was taking on lucrative work overseas when he was supposed to be overseeing the final stretch of the Republican campaign, three people said. One person said Wiles approved the trip without informing Trump, raising questions about how closely she was overseeing his political advisers. For Trump, the larger concern is that Blair's outside work has distracted him from his political responsibilities, two people said. In a statement, Blair said: "All of this mudslinging is ridiculous, and counterproductive. President Trump and me are focused on helping Republicans win in November. Every other Republican should be doing the same." In a separate statement, LaCivita said: "President Trump and his team are and always have been focused on the midterms. That's demonstrated through the money, message and motivation that the president is bringing on the road and all year. Sniping from unnamed cowards who've never been in a fight is not worth responding to." $200 MILLION AND REDISTRICTING With Trump asking why Republican polling in pivotal races has not improved despite MAGA Inc.'s campaign spending, which public records put at $200 million so far, it remains unclear whether he will approve more spending before the election, one of the sources said. Trump also has pressed political aides and advisers in the past week to explain why the redistricting effort he personally pushed has failed to deliver more clear-cut Republican gains, two sources said. Texas is a particular concern. Republicans redrew the state's congressional map to gain seats, but the strategy relies in part on Hispanic voters turning out as they did for the 2024 election. Opinion polls suggest that support may be difficult to replicate amid concerns about the cost of living and Trump's handling of the economy. Some Republicans fear the new boundaries could backfire, leaving incumbents more vulnerable instead of giving the party an advantage. "The redistricting diced up the Trump voters too much," one of the sources said. Trump had said Blair was expected to return to the White House after the midterms, describing his departure as a "short leave of absence." But two sources said his return was now unlikely. "He's not coming back. That is not happening," one of them said. It was less clear how things would play out for Wiles, who played a central role in Trump's 2024 victory and has been credited by Trump allies and aides with bringing greater discipline to his White House in his second term. Trump "may be annoyed at certain things but she has effectively kept that machine going," a fourth source close to the White House said.

item.title: What redistricting means for Tennessee voters
item.description: Redrawing the lines splits neighbors and groups them with people far away.
item.dc:creator: Ally J. Levine, Bianca Flowers, David Hood-Nuño
item.content:encoded: It’s a political fault line that leaves neighbors on both sides with less say. 9th District5th District The street outside Tammy Jo O'Neal's home has become a political boundary with big implications. The city of Memphis used to sit almost entirely in one congressional district. The new map splits O'Neal from neighbors across the street, each now belonging to districts with voters halfway across the state who have different needs and interests. O'Neal sees the new map as more than a split block. “There's this divide that's happening in our lives,not just in our districts.” District 5 District 9 Tammy Jo O’Neal sits for a portrait on the front porch of their home on Elzey Ave in Memphis, Tennessee, US, July 29, 2026. REUTERS/Seth Herald A citydivided By Bianca Flowers , David Hood-Nuño and Ally J. Levine Published Oct. 17, 2026 6:00 a.m. EDT What happens when congressional district lines are redrawn, splitting neighbors and grouping them with people far away Four years before the Memphis redistricting, Republicans used a similar strategy in drawing new maps for Nashville. They split the city, which had voted overwhelmingly Democratic for roughly 70 years, into three broader districts where Republicans can now easily prevail. Battles over redistricting have long been intertwined with racism and political power, particularly in southern states like Tennessee. Sixty-four years ago, a federal court found Tennessee diluted voting power in urban areas where majority Black voters lived and ordered the legislature to redraw its congressional districts. For decades, the Voting Rights Act of 1965 was a powerful tool for Black voters, particularly in the South, to challenge discrimination and protect political power among people of color to elect representatives who would advocate for their communities. The act significantly increased Black and Hispanic representation in Congress by curtailing certain redistricting practices, including splitting people of color among many districts or concentrating them in some districts to limit their impact in others. But those protections have been steadily weakened. In 2013, when Democrat Barack Obama was president, the Supreme Court’s decision on the Alabama case Shelby County v. Holder gutted a provision requiring federal approval before states change voting laws or political maps. In April, the court narrowed the Voting Rights Act further in Louisiana v. Callais , making it harder to challenge new maps that dilute the voting power of communities of color. The court essentially required such challenges to prove that districts were drawn intentionally to discriminate on the basis of race, and not for other reasons. Republicans argue their redistricting in Tennessee and elsewhere is about party politics, not race. They point out that Democrats regularly redraw districts in states they control to give their party easier election wins. Democrats have done the same in California, for example, said Steve Hickey, chair of the Republican Party in Williamson County, a popular suburban area south of Nashville. “This is part of a bigger game being played nationally, and I don’t think it’s fair to say that this was done to gut” the Voting Rights Act, he said. Redistricting in the United States is generally controlled by state legislatures, which adjust voter maps after the once-a-decade census. Both parties have historically used the process to help their candidates win future elections. In 2025, at the urging of President Donald Trump, Texas launched an unusual mid-decade redistricting drive as part of a broader Republican push to gain congressional seats in half a dozen states, including Tennessee. Democrats responded with their own partisan redistricting in California and attempts that faltered in other states. Civil rights activists say Tennessee’s congressional districts, all of which currently favor Republicans, are now a testing ground for dismantling voting rights protections across the United States. “This lack of competition spills over and has racial implications,” said John Geer, a political science professor at Vanderbilt University who conducts polling in Tennessee. Reuters sought to quantify the impact of redistricting on the voters of Tennessee, examining public funding, demographics and socioeconomic factors to show why it’s important to residents when a city is split up like this. MemphisDistrict 9Suburbs of NashvilleDistrict 5District 8District 9 Population by race, one dot per person Black residents White residents Other races and ethnicities Memphis has the largest Black population in Tennessee. The city of some 630,000 people is 63% Black. Memphis accounted for 78% of the former District 9’s population, making it the only majority-Black district in the state. Earlier this year, the Tennessee legislature drew new district lines, splitting Memphis and its Black communities into three separate districts. The pieces of the city are now grouped with rural and suburban Tennesseans in districts that reach halfway across the state. Note: “White” and “Black” are non-Hispanic. “Other races and ethnicities” combines Hispanic or Latino residents of any race with the non-Hispanic categories Asian alone, American Indian and Alaska Native alone, Native Hawaiian and Other Pacific Islander alone, Some Other Race alone, and Two or More Races. Sources: US Census Bureau (2020 census redistricting data; TIGER/Line boundaries); Tennessee Comptroller of the Treasury (2026 districts); All About Redistricting, Loyola Law School (2022 districts); State of Tennessee and the City of Memphis Engineering Division (city limits); Tennessee Department of Transportation (roads) Reuters spoke to more than 35 redistricting scholars, political analysts, civic leaders, political candidates and voters about the consequences of redistricting for the most vulnerable communities in Tennessee’s two biggest cities. Cities faced the biggest impact because rural areas were already represented by a Republican and continue to be so after the redistricting, albeit in districts with different demographics. Before redistricting, both Nashville and Memphis were overwhelmingly Democratic districts in an otherwise Republican state. In 2024, District 9, including most of Memphis, went 71% for Democrat Steve Cohen. In 2020, Jim Cooper, a Democrat, ran unopposed in Nashville’s District 5, winning more than 99% of votes cast. In 2022, the new District 5 flipped, with the Republican candidate winning 57%. Tennessee’s new maps have combined city, suburban and rural populations that have widely varying needs and political preferences. The residents of Nashville and Memphis, for instance, are far more likely to struggle with poverty, housing, public safety and related issues. Residents there could now struggle to elect Congress members who prioritize policies to address these issues, according to Odessa Kelly, executive director of Stand Up Nashville, a nonprofit community organization that advocates for racial and economic equality. She said Black voters in Nashville no longer felt they had someone to stand up for them in Congress, from federal funding going to the city to critical votes on bills that directly affect city residents. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention developed the Social Vulnerability Index to gauge how well a community can withstand and recover from an emergency, and to identify which communities may need the most support. Shelby County, home to Memphis, ranks among the most vulnerable of Tennessee’s 95 counties on various indicators such as housing cost burden and lack of access to a vehicle. Memphis, Nashville residents rank higher in social vulnerability A US government index compares Tennessee communities on socioeconomic and demographic factors gauging their resilience to unexpected hardships. 25th 50th 75th 100th percentile Lower vulnerability Higher vulnerability Shelby County (Memphis) Minority status Racial or ethnic minority 100 Davidson County (Nashville) Housing and transportation In structures of 10+ units 97 No vehicle available 94 More people than rooms 60 Lives in group quarters 56 Mobile homes 0 Household characteristics Aged 17 and under 97 Single-parent household 96 Speaks English less than well 91 With a disability 9 Aged 65 and over 5 Socioeconomic status Housing cost burdened 100 Unemployed 86 No health insurance 76 Below 150% of poverty 50 No high school diploma (25+) 16 0 Chart showing where Shelby County and Davidson County rank among Tennessee’s 95 counties on 16 measures of the CDC’s Social Vulnerability Index, grouped into four themes, on a scale from the 0 to the 100th percentile with the other 93 counties as faint ticks. Both rank high on most measures — Shelby at the 100th percentile for racial or ethnic minority share and housing cost burden, Davidson at the 100th for apartments in large buildings and for people who speak English less than well. Both drop to the middle or bottom on poverty, the 50th percentile for Shelby and the 23rd for Davidson, and on residents aged 65 and over. Source: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry Social Vulnerability Index 2022 In 2024, just over a third of Tennessee voters picked Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris, and in 2020, Democrats won two congressional seats out of the state’s nine, carrying Nashville and Memphis. Now, every congressional district in Tennessee is considered “safe” for Republicans. Sandi Wells, a self-described “very conservative” voter from Williamson County, just outside Nashville, said it was “kind of odd” to group Memphis in the same district with parts of Williamson County 200 miles away. But she rejected the notion that districts should be drawn to protect Black voting power. “I don’t think we should have districts that are based on race,” she said. “I mean, that’s just ridiculous for anyone to even think that we should have that.” Shane Tinnin, a 52-year-old small business owner who maintains homes in both cities and has voted mostly for Democrats, understands that parties seek political power through redistricting but called the Memphis maps a particularly striking setback for Black political power. “In Nashville, it seemed really more like this is a political move,” he said, noting that it was not a Black-majority city. “When you do it in Memphis, where it’s an even more liberal district, but also a predominantly Black district, it just feels especially egregious to me.” Odessa Kelly, executive director at Stand Up Nashville, points to topics of focus for her and her team at a meeting in July. REUTERS/Seth Herald Volunteers for The Equity Alliance canvass through neighborhoods in Memphis to do “accountability” door knocks to speak with residents about elected officials following the GOP-led effort to redistrict the city. REUTERS/Seth Herald Securing funding Reuters examined how Nashville’s redistricting has impacted community project funding, under which lawmakers can seek federal money for local projects. Previously known as earmarks, community project funds returned to Congress with a more transparent process in fiscal year 2022 after a decade-long moratorium. A Reuters analysis found a dramatic shift in funding for Nashville after the city was split among three districts. Jim Cooper, a Democrat, steered most of the old 5th District’s project funding to Nashville in fiscal years 2022 and 2023. In the years since, only a small share of funding has gone toward projects in the city, including fiscal year 2027 requests still pending before Congress. Funding can vary greatly between representatives. Only John Rose, who currently represents the 6th District, has requested funding among the three members whose districts included Nashville after redistricting. Matt Van Epps and Andy Ogles have not pursued community project funding for their districts at all, arguing against such spending on principle. All three did not provide a comment or did not respond to a request to comment. Total Community Project Funding for districts that include Nashville After FY2023 FY2024 $18 mln $21 mln $2.5 mln Not Nashville $18 mln Nashville Nashville $3 mln $15.5 mln Before Two flow diagrams comparing Community Project Funds before and after redistricting. In the year before, when Nashville sat in a single district, District 5 received $18 million and $15.5 million of it went to Nashville, with $2.5 million going elsewhere. In the year after, with Nashville divided across three districts, Districts 5, 6 and 7 received $21 million between them but only $3 million reached Nashville, while $18 million went to areas outside the city. Note: Data show the total funding for districts that include Nashville. Before the 2022 redistricting, Nashville was contained in District 5. After, it was split between Districts 5, 6 and 7. Source: US Government Accountability Office The shift away from community funding jeopardized future funding for projects like public housing, healthcare centers, buildings for the two historically Black colleges in the city and public transportation in Nashville. For Memphis, a similar decline in earmark funding would be a big loss. Since 2022, District 9 Representative Steve Cohen, a Democrat, pulled in $52.6 million for projects based in Memphis, according to figures published by the US Government Accountability Office and the US House Committee on Appropriations. That’s 83% of all the community project funding for District 9 in that period. District 7 State capitol District 6 State House of Representatives The Tennessee State Capitol building and Legislative Plaza, which is undergoing construction. REUTERS/Seth Herald Another important role for a member of Congress is to act as a middleman between people in their district and the government, helping negotiate the bureaucracy of Washington. When Cooper represented Nashville, he fielded calls about immigration paperwork, passports, Medicare, Social Security checks and more, said Tennessee State Senator Charlane Oliver, who worked as a community liaison and communications staffer in Cooper’s congressional office from 2017 to 2019. “He would show up to the cookout, the fish fry, the parades, the meetings and the galas,” she said. That kind of interaction is harder if the representative does not have a local office. When Nashville was split, only one representative, Mark Green of District 7, kept an office near the center of the city. That office was closed when Van Epps took over the seat in 2025, leaving no offices within the city limits. Constituents in Nashville have to drive 36 miles on average to visit a congressional district office, a Reuters analysis found, compared with less than 10 miles when Cooper represented Nashville, the seat of Davidson County. Average trip to Congressional district office District 5 +39 miles after District 6 +17 mi District 7 +16 mi 0 10 20 30 40 50 miles 9 miles before redistricting A chart of the average driving distance for Nashville residents to their closest congressional district office, shown for each of the three districts the city is now split among. A dark bar common to all three marks the 9-mile average from when Nashville sat in a single district, flagged on the scale as “9 miles before redistricting.” A lighter bar extends past it to each district’s new average: District 5 adds 39 miles, reaching about 47; District 6 adds 17, reaching about 25; and District 7 adds 16, reaching about 24 miles. Note: Data shows the average driving distance for Nashville residents in each district to their closest district office. District 7’s offices are those open under Rep. Matt Van Epps, who won the seat after Mark Green resigned in 2025. Green kept an office in downtown Nashville; which put District 7’s average at 5 miles. That office no longer exists. Source: Reuters analysis of congressional district office locations Van Epps and the other two Republicans running this year in Nashville districts, Johnny Garrett and Charlie Hatcher, did not respond to Reuters requests for interviews for this story. Most city buses don’t operate far enough outside the city to visit a congressional district office in Cookeville, more than an hour’s drive away. Kyle Cook, who works in the public library, said Cooper’s office used to be just upstairs from his own in downtown Nashville. “Now, if I wanted to advocate just as a regular citizen for better busing, I would have to call this office in Cookeville and it’s just not the same kind of relationship,” Cook said. Who speaks for Memphis? Cohen represented Memphis for 19 years but stood down when new maps were passed, saying “these districts were drawn to beat me.” State Representative Justin Pearson, a progressive Democrat, is campaigning to represent the 9th District. Pearson gained national attention in 2023 when he was temporarily expelled from the Tennessee House, for what Republicans described as a breach of decorum when he joined a protest on gun control . Polls show him trailing Brent Taylor, a Republican state senator endorsed by President Donald Trump. But Pearson said Tennessee was “not a lost cause” for Democrats. In an interview with Reuters, Pearson described the Memphis redistricting as “one of the most significant political deprivations of Black political power and accessibility to the ballot since the end of Reconstruction in Tennessee.” Tennessee State Representative Justin Pearson stands for a portrait in the Cooper Young neighborhood in Memphis. REUTERS/Seth Herald Taylor has defended redistricting efforts in Tennessee as a “compliance measure” in response to the 2026 US Supreme Court ruling that he says prohibits the consideration of racial data when redrawing political boundaries. Asked about his top priorities in such a diverse district spanning downtown Memphis to rural Fayette County, Taylor pointed to inflation. “Everybody feels the pain right now,” he said. “When I filled up my car the other day, it was $112. People feel the pinch at the gas pump. They feel higher prices when they go to the grocery store. Everything we do costs more.” Civil Miller-Watkins, an eighth-grade math teacher in Fayette County who was drawn into District 9 and plans to vote for Pearson, said the needs of voters in her area differ from those in Memphis. Rural voters worry about access to broadband, ambulances, grocery stores and schools, she said. “All of these interests are very legitimate,” Miller-Watkins said. “But I don’t know if any community can say they’re going to have effective representation.” Pearson, the Democrat, says he’s campaigned in 15 counties that now come under the district and economic hardship is the common thread. “That’s hurting people who are working class in Memphis, just like it’s hurting farmers in Savannah, Tennessee,” he said. “We have a lot more in common.” Urban 96% Suburban 4% Shelby County 737,000 people live in an urban county in District 9 Tipton County 31,000 live in a suburban county District 9 After Urban 35% Suburban 27% Memphis Nashville Williamson 107k Shelby 269k people Rutherford 39k Maury 33k Memphis area Small towns 22% Bedford 50k Lincoln 35k McNairy 26k Giles 30k Hardeman 25k Marshall 34k Lawrence 44k Hardin 27k Wayne 16k Moore 7k Rural 16% Before redistricting Fayette 25k Two panels comparing the counties that make up Tennessee’s 9th Congressional District before and after the 2026 redraw, with each county drawn at an area proportional to its population. Before, the district is almost entirely one place: urban Shelby County, home to Memphis, fills the panel with roughly 737,000 people, beside a thin sliver for suburban Tipton County’s ~31,000. After, 767,872 people are spread across 15 counties in four groups. Urban counties make up 35% of the district; suburban counties comprise 27%, small towns 22% and rural counties 16%. Note: Counties are grouped by the National Center for Health Statistics urban–rural classification. “Large central metro” was renamed to “Urban”, “Large fringe metro” to “Suburban”, “Micropolitan” to “Small towns” and “Noncore” was renamed “Rural” in this graphic. Sources: US Census; NCHS Urban-Rural Classification Scheme; Tennessee Comptroller of the Treasury (2026 district); All About Redistricting, Loyola Law School (2022 district) Pearson said he was concerned that some voters were confused about which district they were in and that this could hurt turnout. Pearson’s advocacy for criminal justice reform and affordability has appealed to younger Democratic Party voters like 27-year-old Marko Jankov. But Jankov, who identifies as a Democratic Socialist, lives in a part of Memphis that was moved out of the 9th District and he said he was less motivated to vote for other Democrats when polls showed them unlikely to win. “They want to make it a psychological thing, where you think you can’t win,” Jankov said. The changes are exposing a rural-urban divide. Debby Gould, president of the non-partisan League of Women Voters of Tennessee, said voters of all backgrounds had concerns. “This is a time when we really have to strengthen urban-rural links and to come up with shared values,” she said. “Because rural voters are also feeling left out on this.” Hickey, the Williamson County Republican chair, said it was up to candidates to show they could work for all their constituents: “They’re going to have to put a lot of miles in their car.” Opening photo Elzey Avenue in Memphis, a dividing line between Congressional District 9 and Congressional District 5, following a Republican-led effort to redistrict Memphis.
